div.head: Northu 50
div.ab: Gif hit si færbena, gilde XII ór.
Gif hit si færbena, gilde XII or.
Wenn es ein gemeinfreier Hintersasse(?) ist, zahle er 12 Ör.
If it is a common freeman tenant(?), let him pay 12 ores.
If it is fœrbena, he is to pay 12 ores.
If he is a commoner, he is to pay twelve oras.
div.note: commoner: The term used here is færbena, a word of uncertain meaning. The similar penalty for wrongdoing indicates that the færbena is equal in status to the cyrlisc man (commoner) and ceorl (peasant) of clauses 53 and 60 and the tunes man (townsman) of clause 59; however, the precise nature of his obligations to his lord remains unclear.

note.seg: Das Wort bezeichnet einen mit cyrlisc man 53, tunes man 59, ceorl 60 identischen Stand. Es glossiert anderwärts erstens epibates, was ursprünglich ‘Schiffsbesteiger, Passagier’, übertragen ‘Mitfahrer im [vom Klerus gesteuerten Kirchen]schiffe, Laie’, dann auch ‘gemeinfreier Kleinbauer’ bedeutet. Die Glossierung ward wahrscheinlich gewählt, weil fær-bena silbenhaft *‘Schiffahrt-Erbitter’ heissen könnte. [Laut freundl. Mitteilung von A. Heusler 1901 lässt sich Nord. beiða fars ‘Schiffahrt erbitten’ (Fritzner Ordbog I 378) vergleichen.] Das andere Lemma für færbena ist saltor, d. i. entweder vermutlich salt(u)arius ‘Flurhüter, Meier, Pächter’ oder aber saltor in nave ecclesiae ‘Laie’. Trotz jener Glossierung kann weder ‘Passagier’ noch ‘Laie’ erklären, wieso ein gemeinfreier Kleinbauer zum Namen færbena kam. Vielleicht ward innerhalb des Bauerstandes dessen höchste Klasse bezeichnet, für die, wie auch sonst bekannt, im Ggs. zur niederen, Herrensuche (s. d. Gl 1a. 3) freistand: also ‘Beansprucher der Freizügigkeit’; s. d. Gl 1a. 4. Für faran, fære (dt, s. Wb) steht der technische Sinn ‘ab-(aus)ziehen des Landbenutzers und Hintersassen von bisheriger Herrschaftszugehörigkeit’ bzw. abstrakt ‘Abzug’ fest; Belege s. Archiv neu. Spra. CXX 337

The word denotes a rank identical with the cyrlisc man of 53, the tunes man of 59 and the ceorl of 60. Elsewhere it glosses, first, epibates, which originally means ‘one who boards a ship, passenger’, figuratively ‘fellow-traveller in the ship [of the Church, steered by the clergy], layman’, and then also ‘common free smallholder’. The gloss was probably chosen because fær-bena, taken syllable by syllable, could mean *‘one who asks for a sea-passage’. [According to a kind communication from A. Heusler in 1901, Norse beiða fars ‘to ask for a passage’ (Fritzner Ordbog I 378) may be compared.] The other lemma for færbena is saltor, i.e. either, presumably, salt(u)arius ‘field-warden, steward, tenant’ or else saltor in nave ecclesiae ‘layman’. Despite that gloss, neither ‘passenger’ nor ‘layman’ can explain how a common free smallholder came by the name færbena. Perhaps it designated the highest class within the peasantry, which, as is also known from elsewhere, was free, in contrast to the lower class, to seek a lord (see that word in Gl 1a. 3): thus ‘one who claims freedom of movement’; see that word in Gl 1a. 4. For faran, fære (dt, see Wb) the technical sense ‘departure (removal) of the occupier of land and dependent tenant from the lordship to which he has hitherto belonged’, or in the abstract ‘departure’, is established; for instances see Archiv neu. Spra. CXX 337

note.label: færbena
note.seg: Apparently the same as the cyrlisc man of chap. 53, the tunesman “villager” of chap. 59, and the ceorl of chap. 60. It must denote a freeman who is not a landowner. By etymology, it should mean “journey-petitioner” and the interpretation in Bosworth-Toller, Supplement, “one who has to ask leave to go from his lord”, which is equivalent to the Domesday Book “could not recede”, seems preferable to Liebermann's interpretation, “one who claims the right to go”, i.e. a higher class of tenant, for this forces the meaning of bena, “a suppliant”. Færbenu glosses epifates, “passengers”, “those who request a passage” in the Erfurt Glossary, which is not very helpful.
